releases.title: Tidier screens and fuller markets
changes: Every screen now follows the facility panel: one typeface, clearer text sizes and no repeated messages, from the top bar and side menu to Supply Chains, Contracts, Reports, Banking, the Build window and dialogs. Settings → Interface size now also scales dialogs.

One speed button replaces the five: click it to go faster, right-click to slow down, or press 1–5. Clicking it while paused starts time again. On phones the money bar now fits the screen in five short columns.

Food is easier to source in new companies: every shop staple starts with independent farms and factories in several towns that sell to anyone, and new food factories come with their own farms instead of buying up the milk, eggs and fruit that shops need. Beef, cheese and egg shops now find suppliers.
The Stocking wizard can stop buying for a purchasing unit: it takes no more deliveries until you choose a supplier again. SKU Intelligence is now called Markets.
Shops supplied by your own farm or factory now get the "sold out: try a higher price" hint, and factory shortage and training advice count deliveries from your own buildings once instead of twice.
Bank loans are repaid over 60 months instead of 24, including loans you already hold, so monthly repayments are smaller.

Founders: a new Agrarian Baron starts with $2,900,000, enough for a farm and a shop it supplies. The Tech Disruptor's Market Intelligence now works (suppliers quote it 10% below their asking price) and its new Motor Freight halves freight on deliveries to its buildings; its digital-quality line, which did nothing, is gone. The Venture Aristocrat's card no longer mentions a dividend mandate, which did not exist.
Mountains sit more naturally in the land: the ground at their foot takes on their colour, and the simpler map used without graphics acceleration no longer shows diagonal bands.

A deposit's card on the map now says who holds it and which mine is extracting it, so a rival's working oil field no longer looks unclaimed. In new games, oil works stand on their oil field instead of beside it.
The Build Facility button steps aside: once you own a building it rests half-visible until you point at it, and it hides while a building panel is open or while you drag the map.

releases.title: Clearer controls and fairer starts
changes: The facility panel is simpler: one status at the top of Overview and Controls says what is wrong and offers the one button that fixes it. Overview holds the key numbers, a one-line layout summary and the monthly report; Controls holds the settings. Long explanations open from "Why?".
The Stocking wizard is now the place to choose what each purchasing unit buys and from whom. Outbound distribution and export routing open from "Shipping & exports".
Settings → Text & interface lets you choose a text size and an interface size, saved in this browser. The facility panel uses one font and clearer sizes; other screens follow in coming updates.

Staff & training shows what your budget buys: skill gained next month, the running cost each skill point adds and what skill changes in that building. It warns when more training will not help because supply or storage is the limit. Staff skill raises the quality of what mines, farms and factories make; units and levels set how much they make.

A factory held back by a scarce input names it, with the numbers, instead of showing "Active", and "Find more" opens the Stocking wizard on the unit that buys it. Warehouses show how full they are, what moved through them last month and what they cost; factories compare what they made with what they sold.
Rival buyers compare suppliers when their yearly contracts renew and may move to a clearly cheaper supplier with stock, so your mines and factories can win customers.
When a product stays in short supply its price still rises, but buyers fall away as it climbs, so prices settle instead of rising without end.

Founders for new companies: the Retail King's town-centre shops draw 15% more shoppers. The Agrarian Baron starts with $2,000,000, pays 20% less on deposit tenders and 15% less for farms. The Master Industrialist starts with $3,200,000 and its shops cost 10% more to run. The Tech Disruptor starts with $1,600,000. The Venture Aristocrat's outside syndicate now holds its 40% from the start. Founder card lines that had no effect were removed.
The map recovers by itself if your graphics driver resets during play.

releases.title: Where you build matters
changes: Where you build now matters. New shops in the town centre can receive more goods and draw more shoppers, with higher land and upkeep costs: a central shop costs $15,000 more in land than one on the edge of town. Inner districts are the middle choice, and shops on the edge keep standard costs.

Deliveries to newly built businesses use the distance between the supplier's site and the buyer's site, including trips within the same town. Site and supplier screens describe the location and show the freight you will pay. Rival companies choose sites and pay under the same rules.
Buildings already standing when you first load this update keep their previous location rules and stay on their existing sites.

Signature headquarters: when you build your Corporate Headquarters you can pick a landmark office of your city and era, such as New York's early tower or London's stone headquarters, on a standard town plot you choose on the map. It changes only the look. The $10M cost, departments, upgrades, overhead and HQ effects stay the same, and you still have one HQ.

Baku gains a walled Old City with painted stone walls and towers, the Double Gates and Salyan Gates, stone streets and a dense quarter of small houses and shops. The taller Maiden Tower stands beside the sea-facing wall, traffic passes through the gate arches and buses stay outside the quarter.
Two-storey courtyard houses with enclosed timber balconies gather around a tree, and Nizami Street gains shop terraces and a carved stone block with projecting window bays and wall lanterns.

Ateshgah fire temple stands with its five-sided enclosure, stone cells, raised entrance and one small flame flickering at the central altar. Philharmonic Hall rises in 1912 with its gold roof, Ismailiyya Palace in 1913, Bibi-Heybat Mosque in 2008 and the three curved Flame Towers in 2012.

Later Baku gains Government House, the Central Bank building, JW Marriott Absheron, Heydar Aliyev Center, Sail tower, Deniz Mall and Crescent Hotel, and Governor's Garden gains its fountain in 2009. Other cities gain New York City Hall, Elizabeth Tower, Birmingham Town Hall, Hôtel Negresco and Tokyo Station, each from its opening year.

Each landmark appears in its own year, with a building site first when it is built during your game. In a saved game, landmarks older than your town appear already finished. Landmarks are protected when you or a rival choose a building site.

More city architecture fills the streets, from Japanese houses, London's high street and New York's loft rows to Art Deco and Streamline buildings, cinemas, schools, hospitals, postwar homes and glass-fronted offices in later decades. Eleven more large designs have rear paintings, so buildings face the streets behind them.

Building sites show painted groundworks and frames before the finished building appears, with two designs for each size. Windmill sails turn, factory loading bays have parked lorries, rural buildings gain short approaches and factories favour paintings suited to what they make.

Country roads and farm tracks take curved bends, town corners are rounded and suitable City Hall crossroads gain roundabouts. Traffic follows the curves, and late-1930s and 1950s cars, lorries and buses join the streets in their eras.
At night, building windows light as whole panes, painted lamps and open furnaces glow, and vehicles have small headlights and red tail lights. Lights follow dusk, dawn and the game clock.

Settings → Map offers High and Low presets, or a Custom mix of Day and night, Night lights, Additional animations and Detailed grass & meadow. Changing them keeps your map view in place. On computers without WebGL, the ground no longer shows thin lines between its tiles.

Map search finds cities and facilities as you type. Layers, My facilities and search share one toolbar, the map controls sit together and Build Facility stays on the map. Pause and the five speed buttons form one group; choosing a speed starts time if the game is paused.

To build, pick a facility type and tap a highlighted lot in any town; you choose the building's design after the site. Tapping empty ground or another building closes the selected facility, and demolishing a facility reports the salvage you recovered.

Facility Controls use folding sections that remember what you opened, with one selling-price editor. On phones, facility panels fill the screen, the money strip scrolls sideways and More holds the extra tools.

The original movable Interactive UI Tour is the only tutorial window; reopen it through More → Tutorial or Menu → Interactive UI Tour. Daily calculations and month-end work run in the background, so the map and controls respond more smoothly.

releases.title: Day and night
changes: Day and night now pass over the map with the game clock. Dusk sweeps across the land from east to west, street lamps light up, and the windows of shops, homes and factories come on one by one. Late at night most of them go dark again.

The sun follows the season: long summer evenings, short winter days. A full day takes about 24 minutes at normal speed, runs faster at higher speeds and stops when the game is paused. Switch it off in Settings for constant daylight.
By day, the painted windows of the buildings no longer glow as if their lights were on.
Town names seen from afar float just above each town in a rounder, see-through label, so you can still see the town itself.
The UI tour and the objectives checklist no longer open on top of each other: the checklist waits until the tour ends.

releases.title: A clearer first hour and Baku landmarks
changes: Baku gains real landmarks, each in its district and in its real year. The Old City's Double Gates and old houses, the historic Governor's Garden and a Nizami Street block stand from the start. The Hajinski house and Mukhtarov Palace rise in 1912, the central department store in 1961, and Park Bulvar and the Hilton on the seafront in the 2010s, each with a building site first. More landmarks follow as their paintings are finished.

A new stocking wizard does product, supplier, volume and contract in one window. Suppliers with goods ready now are listed first with their landed cost (price plus freight), the monthly volume is suggested from what your purchasing unit can take in, and one button signs.
Contract bids now start at the supplier's asking price instead of the market price, and the screen explains when you offer more than the ask.

Shops say exactly where they stand: no product chosen, no supplier contract, waiting for the supplier's stock, deliveries due or arriving, or selling, each with its next step. A signed supplier with nothing to deliver no longer shows a green "Operational".

The top bar shows last month's profit and your runway: how long cash lasts after loan payments. Press Cash for the month's money story: profit, loan principal and interest, the resulting cash change, debt, equity and your stake. Reports and Banking open with the same summary.

The checklist's last goal is now "Next chapter": review your price, sell more of what works, add a second product, open a second shop or make your own goods. Each shows its cost, the cash you would have left, an estimate and, if it is out of reach, how many months of saving it needs. Any paid step completes the chapter.
On the map, your buildings have a gold outline, "My facilities" lists them, and the town name over the map opens its City Hall.
On phones, Cash opens debt, equity and runway; a shop's next stocking step stays at the top of its panel; and "Show map" folds the panel away.
The game starts faster: rarely used windows such as reports, charts and contracts load the first time you open them.
The objectives checklist can be moved on every screen, including phones and narrow windows: drag it by its title bar. It remembers where you put it.
The – button minimises the checklist to a small pill that you can also move. Tap the pill to open the checklist again, or use × to close it.
After you move the checklist with a finger, your next tap on it works straight away. Map menus such as Layers always open above the checklist.

releases.title: Living cities
changes: A new main screen: the map fills the window, the top bar shows cash, 12-month profit, equity, stake, debt and time, and the menu bar opens facilities, supply chains, contracts, reports, banking and news. The objectives checklist floats over the map and can be dragged anywhere.

Every town is drawn street by street with painted buildings in its own architecture. Your buildings, rival businesses, farms, mines and deposits all stand on the map, and street traffic moves with the game speed.
Towns grow with their population, and older districts are gradually rebuilt in the styles of each decade. Company buildings never move.
When you build, choose the building's look, then pick its site on the map or let the game choose. Mines keep their deposit and claim steps.

Select any building to open its controls. Click a town's City Hall and choose "Open city economy" to see local demand. The previous world map is under Layers as "Economic map & overlays", with a box to find a city or facility.
Phones and computers with less memory load lighter map images automatically.
Shops that sold every unit they received, with an empty counter, suggest trying a 5% higher price, up to 1.5 times the local reference price. This is advice only; prices never change by themselves.

Fixes: product landed costs use actual costs when the counter is empty; asking a supplier for a discount can never raise the contract price; a supplier whose contract has ended shows "Linked · no contract" instead of "Contract Linked".
Existing saves gain their city map when loaded, and buildings that already stand keep a neutral site. Money, goods, prices and contract terms are unchanged.

releases.title: A friendlier start
changes: The guide now starts with an affordable shop stocked from a supplier. Building your own farm, mine or factory comes after your first profit.
Survey City opens City Hall on its demand view, and clicking a city on the map also completes that step. New games start paused while the tour explains the screen.
Stores and factories that have no supplier yet show "Waiting for supply" with a hint, instead of "Operational".
Time pauses with a clear notice when company cash first drops below zero, and again if the bank's one-time emergency loan is drawn, showing its cost and what happens next.

New games: every starting farm and mine now has a buyer. Fresh produce and meat have their own shops, and rival companies make beer, chocolate, coffee, soap, cookware, linen shirts, wool sweaters, leather shoes and silver jewelry. Copper, tobacco and tea are left for you or rivals to develop.
Existing saves keep their world. Prices, production rates and contract terms are unchanged.

releases.title: Smoother goods flow
changes: Goods passed through two connected storage units keep moving toward the unit that uses or sells them, instead of being shuffled back and forth.
A general purchasing unit that feeds a recipe with several ingredients shares its daily intake between them in the recipe proportions, so production can start right away.
Customers with signed supply agreements keep their reserved deliveries every day. Your own linked factories no longer take that output on alternate days.
Stores sharing a scarce supplier from your own company record the cost and quality of the goods they actually receive.
Rival companies compare supplier prices with normal market prices as well as with temporary price slumps, so a glut no longer makes them refuse every fair offer.
Existing goods, prices, production rates and contract terms are unchanged.

releases.title: More accurate harvest planning
changes: Farm harvest monitors use the same climate and rainfall rules as production. New expandable guidance explains batch harvests, storage and factory intake.
Crop supply estimates share storage more accurately between growing units instead of treating partly used storage as completely occupied.
Forecasts include the existing Agrarian harvest bonus for your farms only. Actual harvest quantities, growth cycles, storage limits and saved goods are unchanged.

releases.title: More accurate supplier capacity
changes: Supplier estimates no longer reserve some linked internal purchases twice when valid supply agreements already cover them.
Remaining internal needs, per-unit supplier choices and stock promised elsewhere stay protected. Estimates are not guarantees of delivery.
Existing goods, prices, manufacturing rates and contract terms are unchanged.

releases.title: Mobile windows and clearer update notes
changes: Contracts, supplier selection and financial reports adapt their contents to smaller screens. Glossary concepts and explanations stack on phones.
Supply-interruption alerts have clearer text and larger buttons. Trade-flow controls fit narrow maps, and deposit and logistics views have more readable terrain.
Phone map animation does less drawing; maps stop animating behind open popups and hidden panels. Reduced-motion preferences also stop map animation.
What's New, the changelog and the roadmap now show consistent player-focused information, with future plans clearly separated from available features.

releases.title: A clearer interface
changes: product comparisons use readable desktop rows and labelled phone cards. Long company names wrap and scores use concise precision.
Sales and receipt charts display observed unit totals. Pricing has a full-width section, with extra quality, brand and history details expandable.
Facility switching fits narrow panels. Phone financial summaries take less space, and the tools row scrolls sideways to keep every button reachable.

releases.title: More reliable mining offers
changes: Mine supply estimates reflect deposit quality, equipment upgrades and remaining reserves. Empty exhausted mines no longer advertise future production; ready stock can still sell.

releases.title: Everyday personal-care Perfume
changes: Perfume follows everyday personal-care purchasing rates, alongside Soap, Detergent, Shampoo and Toothpaste, rather than slow luxury handling.
Your existing goods and chosen selling prices remain unchanged. Staff training, supplier stock and customer demand still limit sales.

releases.title: Clearer supply problems
changes: Purchasing summaries identify each unit's actual supplier and explain contract deliveries or shortages more accurately.
A supplier with separate stock for its own factories can make more of its public stock available. Goods belonging to warehouse tenants remain protected.

releases.title: Independent suppliers and better price controls
changes: Choose a supplier for each purchasing unit. Several units can share a supplier or use different suppliers; each contributes its own receiving throughput.
Selling-price limits consider current local and national references, so you can match market prices without an outdated ceiling.
Level 1 factory purchasing has a 300-unit monthly base intake, separate from its storage buffer. Training and paid upgrades affect receiving.
Staff and technology quality work consistently through multi-stage manufacturing. Previously produced goods keep their quality.

releases.title: Everyday goods and connected production
changes: Casual Clothing, Work Clothing, Soap, Detergent, Shampoo and Toothpaste have faster trained retail purchasing; luxury apparel and jewelry remain slower.
Manufactured reference prices better reflect usable output. Supply estimates recognise connected intermediate production and shared ingredients.
Internal invoice quotes more accurately identify the transferred product. Profitable livestock suppliers can expand when customers can receive and afford more.

releases.title: Rivals respond to shortages
changes: Rivals can supplement partial supply orders, favour stocked suppliers and adjust wholesale prices in response to finished-goods availability.
Sustained shortages can encourage funded production or livestock expansion when inputs are available.
New business offers consider receiving capacity, existing stock, freight and available funds. An offer does not guarantee delivery.

releases.title: Smoother factory flow
changes: Shared ingredient storage better balances materials. Intermediate goods can pass through storage to downstream manufacturing instead of becoming stranded.
Finished output is less likely to flow backward into ingredient storage. Controls explain receiving throughput separately from storage capacity.

releases.title: Supply quantities and city spending
changes: Propose custom monthly contract quantities with receiving and supply warnings. Editing terms requires fresh agreement.
Warehouse deliveries respect receiving limits and tenant ownership. Existing factory energy payments contribute to the city budget.

releases.title: Competition, warehouses and private labels
changes: Funded rivals can enter profitable city markets and respond to competitors' prices, subject to real supplies and costs.
Supply interruptions pause with an affected-facility warning. Sales contracts can dispatch your ready warehouse stock without changing agreed terms.
Private-label units process connected stock for a fee, preserving quantity, quality and producer information through storage and resale.
The five time speeds progress more evenly. product selection remains stable as daily figures refresh.

releases.title: Store service and everyday shopping
changes: Groceries have faster trained purchasing. Sales staff training improves service, not the quality of the goods themselves.
Customer experience contributes to brand loyalty; staple sales do not require high brand awareness.
Company setup and construction explain unit costs, working capital and starting debt more clearly.

releases.title: Safer finances, saves and bug reports
changes: Improved loan, bond, acquisition and warehouse accounting, including protection for goods held for other companies.
Bug reports and attached saves are private to authorised reviewers. Report submissions do not require a reviewer account.
Save/load errors are shown rather than silently replacing your campaign.

releases.title: A daily economy
changes: Purchasing, production, deliveries, sales, stock and quotes update daily. Facility Controls separates current-month figures from completed monthly reports.
Warehouse and farm storage readouts account for upgraded units. Multiple purchasing units share scarce supply according to their receiving limits.
Efficient pipeline layouts earn saved badges, with milestones for 10, 20 and further groups of ten distinct facilities.
Construction-payback advice supports a chosen recovery period when investment costs are known.

releases.title: Economy modes and price advice
changes: New companies default to Balanced. Deep Simulation is available in Settings; older campaigns retain their mode until you switch.
Price hints estimate operating break-even from recorded sales and expenses. They do not set your price or guarantee customers.

releases.title: Supply chains that start with your purchases
changes: Assign purchasing products before choosing recipes. Connected ingredients determine what each manufacturing unit can make.
Only goods routed to sales or outbound units are offered to other companies; intermediate goods can stay in your own production chain.
Stores sell actual sales-floor stock, with price controls and stranded-stock warnings. Transfers between your own facilities appear in their books.
Stores compete for shared city demand. The Operations Desk places pipelines and facility controls side by side; popups close with Escape.

roadmap.title: Business balance and reliable supply
items: Improve everyday, mid-range and luxury business viability without guaranteeing profit.
Keep long supply chains, rival sourcing and late-game competition responsive to stock, costs and customer demand.
Make shortages, receiving limits and operating costs easier to understand.

roadmap.title: Comfortable play on every screen
items: Continue simplifying crowded windows and improving small-screen controls.
A clearer first hour: suggested starter products for each city and price coaching from real sales.
Improve responsiveness and large-company performance while retaining daily figures.

roadmap.title: Where you build matters
items: Busy central streets versus cheaper outskirts: land, upkeep, shoppers and freight depend on where a new building stands.
Rival companies follow the same rules. Buildings standing before the update keep a neutral site.
Sites are described in words, such as "central" or "edge of town", rather than numbers.

roadmap.title: Living city map
items: Towns drawn street by street in their own architecture, growing and rebuilding over the decades.
A choice of building designs and sites when you build.

roadmap.title: Connected businesses
items: Factories using your chosen ingredients, multi-product stores, per-unit suppliers, warehouses and negotiated supply contracts.
Daily operating figures, monthly reports, price advice and staff training.
Balanced and Deep Simulation modes, rival market entry and private-label production.

roadmap.title: A changing economic world
items: Limited port imports and exports that complement domestic suppliers. Ports are not currently active in the core game.
Government supply tenders and more detailed electricity, gas and water providers with commercial bills.
Deeper links between population, household income, inflation and banking.

roadmap.title: More long-term choices
items: Revisit research, media and advertising options after core business balance is stronger.
Optional historical or random crises, trade policies and scenarios that challenge businesses in different ways.

highlights.title: Tidier screens and fuller markets
highlights.text: Every screen uses one clear typeface and one speed button. New companies find independent food suppliers in every town, bank loans are repaid over 60 months, and the Agrarian Baron and Tech Disruptor get stronger starts.

highlights.title: Clearer facility controls
highlights.text: Each building shows one status with the button that fixes it, numbers on Overview and settings on Controls. Choose your own text and interface size in Settings.

highlights.title: Where you build matters
highlights.text: Central streets bring more shoppers and room for more goods at higher land and upkeep costs, and freight follows the distance between sites. Your headquarters can take a signature design from your city and era.

highlights.title: Living cities
highlights.text: Every town is drawn street by street with painted buildings in its own style. Choose how your new buildings look and where they stand, and watch towns grow and change over the decades.

highlights.title: Phone-friendly business controls
highlights.text: Contracts, finances, suppliers and glossary pages now adapt their contents to smaller screens. Supply alerts and trade-flow panels have clearer, reachable controls.

highlights.title: Less clutter, useful information
highlights.text: Compare product offers in desktop rows or phone cards, use full-width pricing, and expand extra details only when you need them.

highlights.title: Your purchasing units, your suppliers
highlights.text: Choose a product and supplier for each purchasing unit. Share one supplier across several units or diversify; training, upgrades and available stock affect receiving.

highlights.title: Know why a chain stops
highlights.text: Daily figures and clearer delivery messages help identify missing inputs. Ready warehouse stock can supply your sales contracts.

notice: Priorities may change. Future plans are not release-date promises and are not available unless marked Available now.
